crise_rehydratation.titre: Diarrhoea and dehydration: the home-made solution
crise_rehydratation.intro: In a crisis, doubtful water and difficult hygiene cause diarrhoea. The real danger is dehydration, especially in babies, children and elderly people. A rehydration solution can be made with water, sugar and salt.
etapes: The best option: oral rehydration salts (ORS) sachets from the pharmacy. Put some in your kit, especially if you have young children.
Without sachets, the WHO recipe: 1 litre of drinking water (boiled then cooled), 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt. Stir until completely dissolved.
Measure carefully: too much salt is dangerous, especially for a child. Taste it: the solution should be no saltier than tears.
Give it in small sips, often, even if there's vomiting (one spoonful every 1 to 2 minutes). An adult drinks at least a glass after each liquid stool.
Keep eating simple foods as soon as possible (rice, pasta, banana, bread). A breastfed baby keeps feeding.
Make a fresh solution every day and throw away what's left after 24 hours.
attention: In any of these warning cases: call 112 or a doctor. The home-made solution helps you hold on, it doesn't treat the cause.
alerte: Baby under 6 months with diarrhoea or vomiting.
No wee for 6 to 8 hours, very dry mouth, sunken eyes, crying without tears, sunken fontanelle in a baby.
Unusual drowsiness, confusion, difficulty waking the person.
Blood in the stools, high fever, vomiting that prevents drinking anything at all.
Diarrhoea lasting more than 2 to 3 days in an adult, more than 24 hours in a young child.
crise_rehydratation.source: Written for Bivaska based on official recommendations (WHO, Red Cross, civil protection, USDA, CDC). If in doubt about someone's health, call 112.

crise_fievre.titre: Fever and minor ailments without a doctor
crise_fievre.intro: During a crisis, surgeries may be closed or overwhelmed. Knowing how to manage a fever or a common ailment, and above all recognising what can't wait, avoids burdening emergency services needlessly and waiting too long when it's serious.
etapes: Fever: from 38 °C. It helps the body defend itself; it's treated mainly for comfort.
Uncover the person (no thick blankets), keep the room at a mild temperature, give plenty to drink, often.

Medicine: paracetamol is generally the first choice. Follow the leaflet exactly for the dose, the interval between doses and the daily maximum; for a child, the dose depends on their weight: follow the dosing on the box or the syringe.
Never give aspirin to a child or teenager without medical advice.
Cold, sore throat: rest, hot drinks, honey (not before one year old), nose rinses with salt water. They clear up on their own in about a week.
Small wounds: clean with clean water and soap, disinfect, cover with a clean dressing and change it every day. Watch for infection: spreading redness, heat, pus, fever.
Write down the time and dose of every medicine given: in a crisis, you forget quickly.
attention: These signs can't wait: call 112, even if the services are overloaded.
alerte: Baby under 3 months with 38 °C or more.
Purplish spots on the skin that don't fade when you press a glass on them.
Stiff neck, violent headache, confusion, seizures.
Difficulty breathing, bluish lips, chest pain.
Fever lasting more than 3 days, or above 40 °C that doesn't come down with treatment.
crise_fievre.source: Written for Bivaska based on official recommendations (WHO, Red Cross, civil protection, USDA, CDC). If in doubt about someone's health, call 112.

crise_traitements.intro: Insulin, heart or blood-pressure medicines, epilepsy, asthma, thyroid, contraception… A sudden interruption can be more dangerous than the crisis itself. It needs preparing beforehand.
etapes: Make a complete list of your treatments: name, dose, timing, prescribing doctor. Keep it in your kit, on paper, and in “My emergency info” (SOS window).
Ask your doctor and pharmacist how to keep a small supply in advance (one or two weeks). Never stockpile without their advice.
Rotate this supply: use the oldest boxes first, watch the expiry dates (Ready 72 h > Stock).

Insulin and medicines to keep cool: unopened vials go in the fridge; the one in use generally tolerates room temperature for a period stated on the leaflet. In a power cut, keep them in a cool box or insulated bag, never in direct contact with ice, never frozen.
Spare glasses, hearing aids and batteries, measuring equipment (glucose meter, blood-pressure monitor) and their consumables are part of the treatment.

If you depend on an electrical device (oxygen, ventilator, home dialysis): register with your electricity supplier, your medical provider and your local council, and plan with them what happens in a power cut.
attention: Never take someone else's treatment, and don't stop a treatment on your own: some (steroids, anti-epileptics, heart medicines) are dangerous to stop suddenly.
If you've missed a dose or are running out, call a pharmacist: in a crisis, duty pharmacies remain the best resource.
crise_traitements.source: Written for Bivaska based on official recommendations (WHO, Red Cross, civil protection, USDA, CDC). If in doubt about someone's health, call 112.

crise_fragiles.intro: A crisis weighs much more heavily on the youngest and most vulnerable. They need a suitable kit, and above all someone who thinks of them.
etapes: Babies: infant formula for several days and bottled water to prepare it, bottles, nappies, wipes, cream, spare clothes, thermometer, rehydration sachets, paracetamol suited to their weight.
Children: their cuddly toy, a game or a book, snacks they like, a family photo with your number written on the back in their pocket.
Explain the situation in simple, calm words, without lying or dramatising. Children copy adults' calm.
Keep landmarks: mealtimes, bedtime, little rituals. Give them a role (watching the lamp, counting the bottles): feeling useful is reassuring.
Elderly people: treatments, glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, continence pads, a blanket. They feel thirst less and dehydrate quickly: get them to drink regularly.
They cope badly with heat and cold: in a heatwave, a cool place and water; in winter, several layers and a heated room.
Isolated people in your building or street: go and knock. Many victims of heatwaves and severe cold lived alone.
attention: Add everyone's needs in Ready 72 h > Kit (number of babies, children, adults): the list adapts.
crise_fragiles.source: Written for Bivaska based on official recommendations (WHO, Red Cross, civil protection, USDA, CDC). If in doubt about someone's health, call 112.

crise_animaux.intro: Pets are part of the household. Not having planned for them pushes people to stay in a dangerous house or go back into it. Better to organise their kit in advance.
etapes: Food for at least 3 days, ideally a week, in a waterproof box, and their bowls.
Water: allow about 50 to 60 ml per kilo per day for a dog or cat, on top of the household's water.
Lead, collar or harness, carrier for cats and small animals, litter and bags.
Their medicines, their vaccination record, and a recent photo of you with the animal (to prove it's yours if it gets lost).
Check that its microchip is registered with your current phone number.
Find out in advance: not all emergency reception centres accept animals. Find a relative, a boarding kennel or a vet who could look after it.
If you have to evacuate, take it with you if possible. If you really must leave it, don't tie it up: it must be able to escape water or fire. Leave plenty of water and food, and a note on the door.
attention: A stressed animal may bite or run away: keep it on a lead or in a carrier during an evacuation, even if it's usually calm.
crise_animaux.source: Written for Bivaska based on official recommendations (WHO, Red Cross, civil protection, USDA, CDC). If in doubt about someone's health, call 112.

crise_moral.titre: Keeping your spirits up when it lasts
crise_moral.intro: Fear, anger, tiredness, insomnia, difficulty concentrating: these are normal reactions to an abnormal situation. They usually pass with time, but a few habits help you hold on and help others.
etapes: Breathe: breathe in through your nose counting to 4, breathe out slowly through your mouth counting to 6. Repeat for one to two minutes: your heart slows and your thoughts clear.
Keep a routine: times for getting up, meals, small tasks, bed. It gives you a grip on a situation you don't control.
Act on what you can: a list of three useful things for the day, and tick them off. Acting pushes back anxiety.
Sleep as much as possible, even in short bursts. An exhausted mind makes bad decisions.
Get information from official sources two or three times a day, then switch off. Rumours and a flood of horror images wear you out.
Stay connected: talk with your loved ones and neighbours, offer your help. Helping others is one of the best remedies against helplessness.
Avoid alcohol and sleeping pills taken without medical advice: they make anxiety and sleep worse.
Alone for a long time: talk out loud, keep a diary (Bivaska's logbook works for that too), set yourself small goals.
attention: In these cases, talk about it: to someone close, to a doctor, or to a helpline (Belgium: Télé-Accueil on 107; France: 3114; elsewhere: your national crisis or suicide prevention line). In immediate danger: 112.
alerte: Thoughts of dying or harming yourself.
No longer able to eat, sleep or look after yourself for several days.
Nightmares, startle reactions and anxiety that don't ease after a few weeks.
crise_moral.source: Written for Bivaska based on official recommendations (WHO, Red Cross, civil protection, USDA, CDC). If in doubt about someone's health, call 112.

crise_electricite.titre: Long outage: electricity and the freezer
crise_electricite.intro: An outage of several days raises two questions: how to recharge the essentials (phone, lamps, radio) and what to do with the food in the fridge and freezer. Plus a deadly danger: carbon monoxide.
etapes: Recharging: power banks charged in advance, a small solar panel with battery, wind-up torches and radio. Keep the phone in power-saving mode and switch off what you don't need.
The car can charge a phone, engine running, only outdoors, never in a garage even with the door open.
Generator: only in the open air, at least 6 metres from the house, exhaust pointing away from doors and windows. Never in a garage, a cellar, a garden shed or under a canopy.

Never plug a generator directly into a socket in the house: it can feed power back into the grid and kill a technician. Use suitable extension leads, or have a changeover switch installed by an electrician.
Fridge and freezer: keep the doors closed. A full freezer stays cold for about 48 hours, half full for about 24 hours. A closed fridge holds for about 4 hours.

After the outage: freezer food that still contains ice crystals, or has stayed at 4 °C or below, can be refrozen or cooked. Anything else from the fridge (meat, fish, milk, ready meals) that stayed above 4 °C for more than 2 hours goes in the bin.
Tip: a thermometer in the fridge and freezer, and frozen water bottles that fill the space and act as ice packs (then drinking water).
attention: Carbon monoxide is invisible and odourless. Headaches, nausea, dizziness, drowsiness in several people at once: get into the open air immediately and call 112.
Never a barbecue, brazier or combustion space heater in a closed room, a tent or a garage.
If in doubt about a food, throw it away: food poisoning in the middle of a crisis is a real danger.
crise_electricite.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of the USDA (food safety during power outages) and the CDC (generators and carbon monoxide).

fab_charbon.intro: Charcoal is wood heated away from air: it loses its water and gases and becomes almost pure carbon. It burns hot, without flame or smoke, and has many uses besides fire.
etapes: Small quantity (the simplest method): fill a metal tin with a lid (biscuit tin, mess tin) with finger-sized pieces of dry, sound wood, without bark. Preferably hardwoods: beech, oak, hornbeam, ash.
Pierce a single small 2 to 3 mm hole in the lid, close the tin and put it in the middle of good embers.
Smoke, then sometimes a small flame, comes out of the hole: these are the wood gases. Let it be.
When nothing more comes out of the hole (often 20 to 40 minutes), take the tin out of the fire with a stick and plug the hole with earth or a small stone.
Let it cool COMPLETELY, lid closed, for at least an hour. If you open it too early, the air relights the charcoal.
Large quantity: the charcoal burners' clamp or pit (stacked wood, covered with earth, a few days of watching). It's a real craft: keep it for your own land, away from trees, with permission.

What it's for: cooking fuel that burns hot without smoke; char cloth for lighting a fire; a layer of crushed charcoal in a water filter (it improves taste and smell, but doesn't make water safe: always boil it); resin glue (see the sheet); drawing and marking; face camouflage.
Teeth: without toothpaste, rubbing your teeth with a chewed twig is enough. Powdered charcoal doesn't do better: it's abrasive and can wear enamel, and dentists advise against using it regularly.
attention: Home-made charcoal is NOT medical “activated” charcoal: it's useless against poisoning. In case of poisoning, call 112 or the poison centre (in Belgium: 070 245 245). Pharmacy activated charcoal is only taken on their advice.
A bag of warm charcoal can reignite by itself hours later: only store it completely cold, in a metal container.
Never painted, treated, varnished or chipboard wood: it gives off toxic fumes.
A charcoal fire or brazier gives off a lot of odourless carbon monoxide: never in a tent, a car or a closed room.
fab_charbon.source: Written for Bivaska from traditional know-how, checked against current safety knowledge.

fab_colle.intro: With pine or spruce resin, a little charcoal and wax, you get a hard, waterproof glue that you warm up to use: repairing a handle, gluing a point, filling a crack, waterproofing a seam.
etapes: Collect resin that has already oozed and hardened on wounds in pine or spruce trunks. Don't wound a living tree to get it.
Melt it gently in an old tin can, set at the edge of the embers, not in the flames: resin is highly flammable.
Remove bits of bark and debris with a stick (or strain it through a cloth).
Add charcoal ground to a fine powder: about one part charcoal to three or four parts resin. It makes the glue stronger and less brittle.
To make it less brittle in the cold, add a little beeswax or fat (about one part in ten).
Mix well, then wind the warm glue onto the end of a small stick: you have a “glue stick”.
To glue: warm the stick near the embers, spread the glue on both pieces, join them and hold for a few seconds. Binding over the top makes the joint much stronger.
attention: Hot resin sticks to skin and burns like wax: handle it with a stick, never with your fingers.
If it catches fire, smother it with a lid or earth, never with water.
To clean your hands: a little oil or fat, then soap.
fab_colle.source: Written for Bivaska from traditional know-how, checked against current safety knowledge.

fab_cendres.intro: Wood ash mixed with water gives “lye”: an alkaline water that removes grease. Our grandparents washed laundry, greasy dishes and floors this way. It's also the basis for making soap.
etapes: Use white or grey ash from hardwood (beech, oak, ash), completely cold and sieved. Never ash from barbecue charcoal with firelighters, painted or treated wood, printed paper or plastic.
Put about one volume of ash for five to ten volumes of water in a bucket (not aluminium: lye attacks it).
Boil it or let it soak for a day, stirring now and then, then let it settle: the ash sinks to the bottom.
Gently pour off the clear water from the top, strained through a cloth. It feels a little slippery between the fingers: that's normal.
For laundry: soak it in this lukewarm water, scrub, then rinse in clear water. For greasy dishes: scrub with a little damp ash and rinse well.
attention: This water is caustic: it irritates the skin and can seriously damage the eyes. Wear gloves if you have them, and rinse immediately with plenty of water if splashed. In the eye: rinse for 15 minutes and get medical advice.
Never drink it and keep it out of children's reach, in a clearly labelled container.
It damages wool and silk: keep it for cotton and linen.
fab_cendres.source: Written for Bivaska from traditional know-how, checked against current safety knowledge.

fab_savon.intro: Soap comes from a reaction between a fat and an alkali. With very concentrated ash water and animal fat or oil, you get a soft, brown, rustic soap, but one that cleans. It's a slow and somewhat dangerous process: do it calmly, not in an emergency.
etapes: Prepare a very concentrated ash water (see the sheet “Ash water”): pour the same water several times over fresh ash, or reduce it by boiling it for a long time.
Traditional strength test: a fresh egg should float at the surface with only a small part of its shell showing. If it sinks, the lye is too weak.
Prepare the fat: beef or mutton tallow, lard, or vegetable oil. Melt it, strain it to remove any bits.
In a large cast-iron or stainless-steel pot (never aluminium), slowly pour the lye into the hot fat, about two volumes of lye for one volume of fat, stirring constantly with a long stick.
Cook over a low fire, stirring, for one to several hours, until the mixture thickens like a cream and no longer separates into layers.
Pour into a mould (wooden box lined with cloth) and let it harden in the air for at least several weeks: the soap gets milder as it ages.
Before using it on your skin, test it on a small area of your arm: if it stings or reddens, it still contains too much alkali. Then keep it for laundry.
attention: Concentrated lye is very caustic: gloves, long sleeves and eye protection (glasses) are essential, children and animals kept away.
Never lean over the pot: splashes burn skin and eyes. In the eye: rinse for 15 minutes with clean water and call 112.
Home-made soap is unpredictable: without scales or pure lye, you can't guarantee it's gentle on the skin. Don't use it on a wound or on a baby.
fab_savon.source: Written for Bivaska from traditional know-how, checked against current safety knowledge.

fab_saponaire.intro: Soapwort (Saponaria officinalis) contains saponins, substances that foam in water and clean gently. It's nature's simplest soap, with nothing dangerous to handle.
etapes: Recognising it: a plant 30 to 80 cm tall, on path edges, banks and riversides. Upright stems, opposite leaves in an elongated oval with 3 clearly visible veins. In summer, clusters of pale pink five-petalled flowers, fragrant in the evening.
Pick a handful of leaves and stems (the root is even richer, but leave the plant in place).
Crush or cut them, then rub them vigorously in a little water between your hands: a light foam appears.
For more foam: boil a handful of the chopped plant in a litre of water for 15 to 20 minutes, let it cool and strain. This liquid washes hands, body and delicate laundry.
Rinse with clear water, away from streams.
attention: Don't drink or eat it: saponins irritate the digestive tract.
Keep it away from your eyes: it stings.
If you're not sure of the identification, don't use it: if in doubt, ash or plain water are safer.
Even “natural”, foam pollutes a stream: wash at least 60 metres from water.
fab_saponaire.source: Written for Bivaska from traditional know-how, checked against current safety knowledge.

fab_bougie.intro: Before paraffin, people lit their homes with tallow, melted animal fat. With fat from cooking and a bit of cotton, you can make a candle or a small lamp that gives light for several hours.
etapes: Collect fat: beef or mutton tallow (the hardest), lard, or cooled cooking fat. Melt it gently and strain it through a cloth to remove bits of meat.
Wick: a strand of pure cotton (string, shoelace, twisted strip of cotton T-shirt). First dip it in the melted fat and let it harden: it will stand upright.
Candle: fix the wick to the bottom of a small metal pot or thick glass jar (a clean tin can, a jar), keep it upright with two twigs laid across the rim, then pour in the melted fat.
Let it set somewhere cool for several hours before lighting. Trim the wick to about 1 cm.
Quick lamp: a shell or small container filled with fat, a wick lying in it with its end sticking out over the rim.
attention: Tallow smokes a little and smells of cooking: air the room.
Never leave it burning unattended, or while you sleep, and put it on a surface that can't burn.
A candle doesn't heat a room: it gives light. To keep warm, wrap up; no improvised fire in a closed room.
The smell of fat attracts animals: on a bivouac, store leftovers away from the tent.
fab_bougie.source: Written for Bivaska from traditional know-how, checked against current safety knowledge.
